prompt: What is the R–O–H bond angle in methanol, in degrees?
explanation: The R–O–H bond angle has an approximately tetrahedral value, 108.5° in methanol, and the oxygen atom is sp3-hybridized, much as in water.

prompt: What is the hybridization of the oxygen atom in an alcohol such as methanol?

choices.text: sp3
sp2
choices.why: An sp2 oxygen would give bond angles near 120°. The R–O–H angle in methanol is 108.5°, nearly tetrahedral.

choices.text: sp
choices.why: An sp oxygen would give a linear, 180° arrangement, far from the 108.5° R–O–H angle.

choices.text: Unhybridized, using pure p orbitals
choices.why: Pure p orbitals would give 90° angles. The R–O–H angle is approximately tetrahedral.

explanation: Alcohols and phenols have nearly the same geometry around oxygen as water: the R–O–H angle is approximately tetrahedral (108.5° in methanol), and the oxygen atom is sp3-hybridized.

prompt: 1-Propanol (MW = 60) boils at 97 °C, while butane (MW = 58) boils at −0.5 °C and chloroethane (MW = 65) at 12.5 °C. What explains the alcohol's much higher boiling point?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between the –OH hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another
1-Propanol has a much higher molecular weight than the other two
choices.why: The three compounds have similar molecular weights (58 to 65), so weight can't explain the difference.

choices.text: Covalent bonds between 1-propanol molecules must break when it boils
choices.why: Boiling separates whole molecules. What must be overcome are weak intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.

choices.text: Its oxygen is sp2-hybridized, which makes the molecule flat
choices.why: The alcohol oxygen is sp3-hybridized. The boiling point is raised by hydrogen-bonding, not by shape.

explanation: A positively polarized –OH hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of another. These hydrogen bonds must be overcome before a molecule can enter the vapor, so 1-propanol boils at 97 °C, far above butane (−0.5 °C) and chloroethane (12.5 °C) of similar molecular weight.

prompt: How many degrees Celsius higher is the boiling point of 1-propanol (97 °C) than that of butane (−0.5 °C)?
explanation: 97 °C − (−0.5 °C) = 97.5 °C. The two compounds have similar molecular weights (60 and 58); the difference comes from hydrogen-bonding in the alcohol.

prompt: 1-Butanol boils at 117.5 °C, 2-butanol at 99.5 °C, and 2-methyl-2-propanol at 82.2 °C. What accounts for the drop as the OH-bearing carbon becomes more substituted?

choices.text: Hydrogen-bonding is more difficult in more hindered alcohols
The more substituted isomers have lower molecular weights
choices.why: All three are isomers, C4H10O, with the same molecular weight.

choices.text: The more substituted isomers are stronger acids
choices.why: Acidity doesn't set the boiling point. In any case, more substituted alcohols such as tert-butyl alcohol are weaker acids.

choices.text: Only primary alcohols can form hydrogen bonds
choices.why: All three have an –OH group and can hydrogen-bond. Crowding around the –OH just makes it harder.

explanation: The three alcohols are isomers, so molecular weight is the same. As the OH-bearing carbon becomes more substituted, the –OH group is more hindered and hydrogen-bonding is more difficult, so less energy is needed to reach the vapor and the boiling point falls (Exercise 17.2.1).

prompt: By how many degrees Celsius does the boiling point of 1-butanol (117.5 °C) exceed that of 2-methyl-2-propanol (82.2 °C)?
explanation: 117.5 °C − 82.2 °C = 35.3 °C. The two are isomers; the hindered –OH of the tertiary alcohol hydrogen-bonds less easily (Exercise 17.2.1).

prompt: What do alcohols form when they act as weak bases and are protonated by a strong acid?

choices.text: Oxonium ions, ROH2+
Alkoxide ions, RO−
choices.why: An alkoxide forms when the alcohol acts as an acid and loses its –OH proton.

choices.text: Phenoxide ions, ArO−
choices.why: A phenoxide is the anion left when a phenol loses its proton.

choices.text: Carbanions, R−
choices.why: Protonation adds H+ to the oxygen lone pair; nothing is removed from carbon.

explanation: Like water, alcohols and phenols are both weakly basic and weakly acidic. As weak bases, they are reversibly protonated by strong acids to yield oxonium ions, ROH2+.

prompt: When an alcohol acts as a weak acid in dilute aqueous solution, what does it produce?

choices.text: H3O+ and an alkoxide ion, RO−
OH− and an oxonium ion, ROH2+
choices.why: That would be the alcohol acting as a base. As an acid it gives its –OH proton to water.

choices.text: H3O+ and a carbocation, R+
choices.why: The O–H bond breaks, not the C–O bond, so the oxygen keeps the negative charge in RO−.

choices.text: H3O+ and a phenoxide ion, ArO−
choices.why: Phenoxide ions come from phenols. An alcohol gives an alkoxide ion.

explanation: As weak acids, alcohols and phenols dissociate slightly in dilute aqueous solution by donating a proton to water, giving H3O+ and an alkoxide ion, RO− (or a phenoxide ion, ArO−, from a phenol).

prompt: Compound A has pK_a = 12 and compound B has pK_a = 16. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: A has the larger K_a and is the stronger acid
B has the larger K_a and is the stronger acid
choices.why: A larger pK_a means a smaller K_a, so B is the weaker acid.

choices.text: A has the larger K_a but is the weaker acid
choices.why: A larger K_a always means a stronger acid.

choices.text: They are about equally strong, because both pK_a values are well above 7
choices.why: Each pK_a unit is a factor of 10 in K_a, so a 4-unit gap is a 10^4-fold difference.

explanation: Since pK_a = −log K_a, a compound with a smaller pK_a has a larger K_a and is more acidic. A (pK_a = 12) is the stronger acid; B (pK_a = 16) is weaker.

prompt: According to Table 17.2.1, how do methanol, ethanol, and tert-butyl alcohol compare in acidity with water?

choices.text: Methanol and ethanol are about as acidic as water, but tert-butyl alcohol is somewhat weaker
All three are about a million times more acidic than water
choices.why: That is how phenols compare with alcohols. Methanol (15.54) and ethanol (16) have pK_a values close to water's 15.74.

choices.text: tert-Butyl alcohol is the most acidic of the three
choices.why: tert-Butyl alcohol has the largest pK_a (18), so it is the weakest acid of the three.

choices.text: Methanol and ethanol are much weaker than water, but tert-butyl alcohol is stronger
choices.why: It's the other way around: tert-butyl alcohol (pK_a = 18) is weaker than water (15.74), and methanol and ethanol are close to water.

explanation: Table 17.2.1 gives pK_a values of 15.54 for methanol, 15.74 for water, 16 for ethanol, and 18 for tert-butyl alcohol. Simple alcohols are about as acidic as water; the more highly substituted tert-butyl alcohol is somewhat weaker.

prompt: Why is tert-butyl alcohol (pK_a = 18) a weaker acid than methanol (pK_a = 15.54)?

choices.text: Its hindered alkoxide ion is less easily solvated by water, so it is less stable
Its alkoxide ion is resonance-stabilized, so it holds on to the proton more tightly
choices.why: Neither alkoxide ion is resonance-stabilized, and resonance stabilization of the anion would make an alcohol more acidic, not less.

choices.text: Methoxide ion is more hindered, so water solvates it more easily
choices.why: It's the reverse: methoxide's oxygen is sterically accessible and easily solvated, which stabilizes it.

choices.text: tert-Butyl alcohol can't hydrogen-bond to water
choices.why: It can. The effect that matters is on the alkoxide ion, which is hard for water molecules to reach and solvate.

explanation: The effect of alkyl substitution on alcohol acidity is due mainly to solvation of the alkoxide ion. The oxygen of methoxide is sterically accessible and easily solvated by water; the oxygen of tert-butoxide is hindered, less easily solvated, and therefore less stable, so tert-butyl alcohol is less acidic.

prompt: Why is 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (pK_a = 12.43) more acidic than ethanol (pK_a = 16)?

choices.text: Electron-withdrawing fluorines spread the alkoxide ion's charge over a larger volume
The fluorines donate electrons to the oxygen and strengthen the O–H bond
choices.why: Halogens are electron-withdrawing here. A stronger O–H bond would make the alcohol less acidic, not more.

choices.text: The trifluoroethoxide ion is resonance-stabilized through its C–F bonds
choices.why: The book explains this as an inductive effect, not resonance.

choices.text: Trifluoroethanol forms stronger hydrogen bonds than ethanol in the liquid
choices.why: Hydrogen-bonding in the liquid affects boiling point. Acidity depends on how stable the alkoxide ion is.

explanation: Inductive effects matter in alcohol acidity. Electron-withdrawing halogen substituents stabilize an alkoxide ion by spreading the charge over a larger volume, which makes the alcohol more acidic: ethanol has pK_a = 16, but 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol has pK_a = 12.43.

prompt: Ethanol has pK_a = 16 and 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol has pK_a = 12.43. To two significant figures, how many times larger is the K_a of trifluoroethanol?
explanation: The pK_a values differ by 16 − 12.43 = 3.57 units, so the K_a values differ by a factor of 10^3.57 ≈ 3.7 × 10^3. That matches the book's statement that trifluoroethanol is approximately 3700 times stronger than ethanol.

prompt: Replacing all nine hydrogens of tert-butyl alcohol (pK_a = 18) with fluorine gives nonafluoro-tert-butyl alcohol (pK_a = 5.4). By how many pK_a units is the pK_a lowered?
explanation: 18 − 5.4 = 12.6 pK_a units. The electron-withdrawing fluorines stabilize the alkoxide ion inductively, making the alcohol far more acidic.

prompt: Which of these bases would NOT convert an alcohol into its alkoxide ion to any useful extent?

choices.text: Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3
Sodium hydride, NaH
choices.why: NaH is a strong base; methanol and NaH give sodium methoxide.

choices.text: Sodium amide, NaNH2
choices.why: NaNH2 is a strong base; ethanol and NaNH2 give sodium ethoxide.

choices.text: Methylmagnesium bromide, CH3MgBr
choices.why: Grignard reagents are strong bases; cyclohexanol and CH3MgBr give bromomagnesium cyclohexanolate.

explanation: Because alcohols are weak acids, they don't react with weak bases such as amines or bicarbonate ion, and they react only to a limited extent with metal hydroxides such as NaOH. They do react with alkali metals and with strong bases such as NaH, NaNH2, and Grignard reagents (RMgX).

prompt: What forms when ethanol is treated with sodium amide, NaNH2?

choices.text: Sodium ethoxide
An oxonium ion, CH3CH2OH2+
choices.why: Oxonium ions form when a strong acid protonates an alcohol. NaNH2 is a strong base.

choices.text: No reaction, because alcohols are too weakly acidic to react with any base
choices.why: Alcohols don't react with weak bases, but strong bases such as NaNH2 do remove the –OH proton.

choices.text: Ethane and sodium hydroxide
choices.why: NaNH2 removes the acidic O–H proton. The C–O bond stays intact.

explanation: Alcohols react with strong bases such as sodium hydride, sodium amide, and Grignard reagents. Ethanol and NaNH2 give sodium ethoxide, an alkoxide; alkoxides are named systematically with the -ate suffix (ethanolate), and are often used as bases themselves.

prompt: Phenol has pK_a = 9.89 and ethanol has pK_a = 16. By how many pK_a units is phenol the stronger acid?
explanation: 16 − 9.89 = 6.11 pK_a units, a K_a ratio of 10^6.11 ≈ 1.3 × 10^6. That is why phenols are described as about a million times more acidic than alcohols.

prompt: How can a phenol often be separated from a mixture with neutral organic compounds?

choices.text: By extracting it into dilute aqueous NaOH, then reacidifying the solution
By extracting it into dilute aqueous HCl, then adding base
choices.why: Acid doesn't deprotonate a phenol. The extraction works because phenols are acidic enough to dissolve in aqueous NaOH as phenoxide ions.

choices.text: By extracting it into dilute aqueous NaOH, then adding more NaOH to bring the phenol back
choices.why: More base keeps the phenol in solution as phenoxide. Reacidification turns it back into the phenol.

choices.text: It can't be separated this way, because phenols are no more acidic than alcohols
choices.why: Phenols are about a million times more acidic than alcohols, which is what makes the basic extraction possible.

explanation: Phenols are about a million times more acidic than alcohols, so they dissolve in dilute aqueous NaOH as sodium phenoxide. A phenol can therefore often be separated from a mixture by basic extraction into aqueous solution, followed by reacidification.

prompt: Why are phenols more acidic than alcohols?

choices.text: The phenoxide anion is resonance-stabilized, with its negative charge delocalized over the ortho and para ring positions
The phenoxide anion keeps its negative charge concentrated on oxygen, where it is held most tightly
choices.why: That describes an alkoxide such as CH3O−. In phenoxide, the charge is spread onto the aromatic ring.

choices.text: The phenoxide anion is resonance-stabilized, with its negative charge delocalized over the meta ring positions
choices.why: Delocalization puts the charge at the ortho and para positions, not meta.

choices.text: Phenols are protonated by strong acids more easily than alcohols are
choices.why: Protonation is about basicity. Acidity depends on how stable the anion is after the proton leaves.

explanation: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide anion is resonance-stabilized. Delocalization of the negative charge over the ortho and para positions of the ring stabilizes the anion and lowers ∆G° for dissociation (Figure 17.2.2).

prompt: Is p-hydroxybenzaldehyde more or less acidic than phenol, and why?

choices.text: More acidic, because the carbonyl group is electron-withdrawing and stabilizes the phenoxide anion
Less acidic, because the carbonyl group is electron-donating and destabilizes the phenoxide anion
choices.why: A carbonyl group is electron-withdrawing (Section 16.4). p-Hydroxybenzaldehyde has pK_a = 7.9, below phenol's 9.89.

choices.text: Less acidic, because the carbonyl group concentrates the negative charge on the phenoxide oxygen
choices.why: Electron-withdrawing substituents delocalize the charge, which makes a phenol more acidic.

choices.text: About equally acidic, because a para substituent is too far from the –OH to matter
choices.why: Para substituents strongly affect phenol acidity. Here the pK_a drops from 9.89 to 7.9.

explanation: Electron-withdrawing substituents make a phenol more acidic by stabilizing the phenoxide anion; electron-donating substituents make it less acidic. A carbonyl group is electron-withdrawing, so p-hydroxybenzaldehyde (pK_a = 7.9) is more acidic than phenol (pK_a = 9.89) (Worked Example 17.2.1).

prompt: p-Nitrophenol has pK_a = 7.15 and phenol has pK_a = 9.89. To two significant figures, how many times larger is the K_a of p-nitrophenol?
explanation: The pK_a values differ by 9.89 − 7.15 = 2.74 units, so the K_a ratio is 10^2.74 ≈ 550. A nitro group at the ortho or para position has a particularly noticeable acidifying effect.

prompt: Which list puts (CH3)2CHOH, HC≡CH, (CF3)2CHOH, and CH3OH in order of increasing acidity?

choices.text: HC≡CH < (CH3)2CHOH < CH3OH < (CF3)2CHOH
(CH3)2CHOH < HC≡CH < CH3OH < (CF3)2CHOH
choices.why: Acetylene is a much weaker acid than any of these alcohols, so it comes first.

choices.text: HC≡CH < CH3OH < (CH3)2CHOH < (CF3)2CHOH
choices.why: More alkyl substitution makes an alcohol less acidic (its alkoxide is harder to solvate), so 2-propanol is weaker than methanol.

choices.text: (CF3)2CHOH < CH3OH < (CH3)2CHOH < HC≡CH
choices.why: This is the reverse order. The electron-withdrawing CF3 groups make (CF3)2CHOH the strongest acid of the four.

explanation: Acetylene is the weakest acid. Among the alcohols, the more substituted 2-propanol is weaker than methanol (its alkoxide is less easily solvated), and the six fluorines of (CF3)2CHOH stabilize its alkoxide inductively, making it the strongest: HC≡CH < (CH3)2CHOH < CH3OH < (CF3)2CHOH (Exercise 17.2.2).

prompt: Which list puts phenol, p-methylphenol, and p-(trifluoromethyl)phenol in order of increasing acidity?

choices.text: p-Methylphenol < phenol < p-(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Phenol < p-methylphenol < p-(trifluoromethyl)phenol
choices.why: A methyl group is electron-donating, so p-methylphenol (pK_a = 10.17) is less acidic than phenol (9.89).

choices.text: p-(Trifluoromethyl)phenol < phenol < p-methylphenol
choices.why: This is the reverse order. The electron-withdrawing CF3 group makes its phenol the most acidic.

choices.text: p-Methylphenol < p-(trifluoromethyl)phenol < phenol
choices.why: An electron-withdrawing CF3 group makes a phenol more acidic than phenol itself, not less.

explanation: Electron-donating groups concentrate the charge and make a phenol less acidic; electron-withdrawing groups delocalize it and make a phenol more acidic. The electron-donating methyl gives p-methylphenol (pK_a = 10.17), and the electron-withdrawing CF3 group makes p-(trifluoromethyl)phenol the strongest (Exercise 17.2.2).

prompt: Which list puts benzyl alcohol, phenol, and p-hydroxybenzoic acid in order of increasing acidity?

choices.text: Benzyl alcohol < phenol < p-hydroxybenzoic acid
Phenol < benzyl alcohol < p-hydroxybenzoic acid
choices.why: Benzyl alcohol is an alcohol: its –OH is not on the ring, so its alkoxide isn't resonance-stabilized by the ring as phenoxide is. It is the weakest of the three.

choices.text: Benzyl alcohol < p-hydroxybenzoic acid < phenol
choices.why: p-Hydroxybenzoic acid has a carboxylic acid group, which is more acidic than a phenol –OH.

choices.text: p-Hydroxybenzoic acid < phenol < benzyl alcohol
choices.why: This is the reverse order. Benzyl alcohol, a simple alcohol, is the weakest acid.

explanation: Benzyl alcohol is an ordinary alcohol, phenols are about a million times more acidic than alcohols, and p-hydroxybenzoic acid carries a carboxylic acid group, more acidic still: benzyl alcohol < phenol < p-hydroxybenzoic acid (Exercise 17.2.2).

prompt: p-Nitrobenzyl alcohol is more acidic than benzyl alcohol, but p-methoxybenzyl alcohol is less acidic. Why?

choices.text: The electron-withdrawing nitro group stabilizes the alkoxide ion, while the electron-donating methoxyl group destabilizes it
The nitro group is electron-donating, while the methoxyl group is electron-withdrawing
choices.why: It's the other way around: nitro is electron-withdrawing and methoxyl is electron-donating.

choices.text: The nitro group hydrogen-bonds to the –OH group, which makes its proton easier to remove
choices.why: The explanation is electronic: how each substituent affects the stability of the alkoxide ion.

choices.text: Both groups are electron-withdrawing, but the methoxyl group blocks solvation of the alkoxide ion
choices.why: The methoxyl group is electron-donating, and that is what destabilizes the anion.

explanation: Substituents that withdraw electrons stabilize an anion and increase acidity; those that donate electrons destabilize it. The nitro group stabilizes the p-nitrobenzyl alkoxide ion, and the methoxyl group destabilizes the p-methoxybenzyl alkoxide ion (Exercise 17.2.3).
